author: Alex Cameron
title: Lankford and Mullin on abrupt cancellation of Trump-Putin summit - NewsBreak
text:
By Alex Cameron ,
11 hours ago
The White House Tuesday announced that a second summit between President Trump and Russian President Putin to help bring an end to the war between Russia and Ukraine has been called off. No specific date had been set for the meeting but the men had agreed to have it in Budapest, Hungary. Asked by reporters about the cancellation, Trump said he didn't want to have a "wasted meeting" but said he still thought he would be able to negotiate an end to the fighting.
Senators James Lankford and Markwayne spoke about the developments with Griffin Media.
LANKFORD : "The challenge with Ukraine and Russia and trying to reach a peace agreement has always been Vladimir Putin. He has been the problem from the very beginning; he is the one who invaded and murdered his neighbors, he is the one who is still intent on being able to murder and dominate his neighbors. So, bringing both sides together to be able to talk, having individual conversations are all positive things, but the issue is still, at the end of the day, Vladimir Putin. If he continues to be able to desire to murder his neighbors, then you've got to be able to find ways to be able to make that stop. So the president's focus right now is how to cut off his flow of money that he has currently to be able to feed his war machine. That’s cutting off the sale of oil to different countries -- he’s working with India to get them to stop buying, working with China to get them to start slowing down their purchasing of Russian oil...slowing down the Russian war machine is the best we can do at this point in trying to be able to stop them from this war."
...on whether the United States should provide Tomahawk missiles to Ukraine: LANKFORD : "The U.S. should supply Ukraine with what Ukraine needs to be able to stop this war. It is helpful for the entire region. if Ukraine has a need to be able to say, to defend ourselves and be able to stop the bloodshed, this weapon system would be helpful. I’ve been supportive of that from the very beginning. I was one of the people pushing President Biden to be able to provide the F-16's faster to Ukraine; they asked for those for over a year before President Biden would actually give those to them, so the weapon systems that Ukraine needs to actually end this war is better for the entire region.
...on whether Senate leadership is discussing moving ahead with the Russia sanctions bill: LANKFORD : "Yeah, we still are talking about the sanctions bill. The president has asked us to be able to hold on it, to say there is a moment in time when that’s the best thing to be able to do. The sanctions bill itself is a sanctions regime much higher than what the president already put onto, for instance, India and other countries as well. So he’s saying there is a time for that hammer to be able to come down, but it’s best for him right now in negotiations to say Congress could do this at a moment, rather than it’s already imposed."
...on why the summit was cancelled: MULLIN : "We think that things are moving in the right direction. We’re still dealing with Putin, who has signaled multiple times he wants to bring an end to the war, but he’s not willing to negotiate at the end of the day. Right now, it seems like there’s more movement on his side and on Zelenskyy‘s side than there’s been in a long, long time. So, we want to give ourselves a little bit more time to work out some details because, ideally, when we go into a summit, we’d like to come out with positive news, if possible. If not, it may just be the next step. From the president’s perspective, we’ve had a lot of these talks before and they haven’t been productive, and he cannot stand meeting just for the sake of meeting. He’s a man of action, which is why he loves making deals and so, if it doesn’t look like there can be a positive outcome with a summit, the summit may not take place."
Alex Cameron Alex Cameron is Griffin Media’s Washington Bureau Chief, reporting from our nation’s capital on issues that impact Oklahomans. An award-winning journalist, Alex first joined the News 9 team in 1995, and his reporting has taken him around the world, covering stories in Bosnia, Colorado, Washington, D.C., Seattle, New York and Ukraine.
